e.etymology: A vintage American name most used in the 1890s. Its source is unclear; it has been explained as a short form of names ending in -zella or -cella, such as Rozella and Marcella.

assoc.t: Zella, Nordstrom's activewear line

e.etymology: The Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Bernard, from the Germanic name Bernhard: bear plus hard, brave or strong.
namesakes: Bernardo (leader of the Sharks in West Side Story)
Bernardo Silva (Portuguese soccer star)
Bernardo Bertolucci (Italian film director)

e.etymology: The Medieval Latin name for Wales, from Welsh Cymry, the name the Welsh use for themselves. It is a doublet of Cumbria and of Cymru.

assoc.t: Cambria, a serif font that ships with Microsoft Office
Cambria quartz countertops
Cambria, coastal town in central California

e.etymology: From Persian arman, an ideal, wish or longing. The name is also common in Armenia and Kazakhstan, and in some languages it is a short form of Armand.
From Arabic sultan, authority or power, which became the title of Muslim sovereigns. It is a given name across the Arab world, Turkey and Central and South Asia.

assoc.t: sultan, the title of a Muslim sovereign

e.meaning: form of Leah, traditionally read as weary
e.etymology: A form of the Biblical name Leah, reached through Russian Liya and also used in Ethiopia and India. Leah is Hebrew and is traditionally read as weary.

e.meaning: pet form of Elaine, a French form of Helen
e.etymology: A respelling of Lainey, a pet form of Elaine, the Old French form of Helen. Lainey and its spellings have climbed quickly in the 2020s.

e.meaning: son of Colin; also an Irish surname meaning young hound
e.etymology: A K respelling of Collins, an English surname meaning son of Colin, a medieval pet form of Nicholas, and an anglicized form of Irish Ó Coileáin, from a word for a young hound.
A pet form of Letitia, from Latin laetitia, joy or gladness, and of its medieval English form Lettice. Among Spanish speakers it is short for Leticia.
namesakes: Letty Ortiz (Michelle Rodriguez's character in the Fast & Furious films)

assoc.t: Letty Ortiz of the Fast & Furious films

e.meaning: short form of Lorenzo, man from Laurentum
e.etymology: The Italian short form of Lorenzo, from Latin Laurentius, a man from Laurentum, an ancient town near Rome whose name was linked with laurus, the laurel.
namesakes: Renzo Piano (Italian architect of the Pompidou Centre and the Shard)

e.etymology: The Scandinavian and Slavic spelling of Christina, from Latin Christiana, a follower of Christ, which goes back to Greek khristos, anointed.
In the US mainly a spelling of Monty, the short form of Montgomery and Montague, both Norman names built on mont, hill. It also matches Spanish and Italian monte, mountain.

assoc.t: monte, a card game, as in the three-card monte street con

e.etymology: From Hebrew Ya'ir, he will light up, from the root for light. In English Bibles he is Jair, a judge of Israel; the Yair spelling is common in Israel and in Latin America.
A medieval English form of Randolph, from Germanic rand, the rim of a shield, and wulf, wolf. It survived as a surname and came back as a first name in the 20th century.
namesakes: Randall Pearson (Sterling K. Brown's character on This Is Us)
Randall Cunningham (NFL quarterback)
Randall Park (actor in Fresh Off the Boat)

assoc.t: Randall Boggs, the chameleon villain of Monsters, Inc.

e.etymology: From Sanskrit kirana, a ray or beam of light. It is given to both boys and girls in India and Nepal, and sounds close to the unrelated Irish name Kieran.
The English word lake, from Latin lacus by way of Old French. It is also an English surname for someone who lived by a lake or stream, and it has joined River and Brooks among the water names.
namesakes: Lake Bell (actress and director)

e.meaning: of the Julius family, a Roman clan name
e.etymology: A form of Juliana, written with the Y of Russian Yuliana and of Latin American Spanish spelling. Juliana is the feminine of Julianus, from the Roman family name Julius.
A French feminine pet form of Paul, from the Roman family name Paulus, Latin for small or humble. English speakers borrowed it in the 20th century.
namesakes: Paulette Goddard (film star of the 1930s and 1940s)

e.etymology: The English word queen, from Old English cwen, a woman or a king's wife. As a given name it was most used in the US around 1900, alongside Queenie.
namesakes: Queen Latifah (rapper and actress)

assoc.t: queen, the title of a female monarch
Queen, Freddie Mercury's British rock band
queen, slang praise for a woman; also drag queen

e.note: It is a title as well as a name and a slang word of praise, so expect Your Majesty jokes.

e.etymology: A run-together form of Mary Jane, long one of the commonest double names in English. Mary comes from Hebrew Miriam; Jane is a feminine form of John, God is gracious.

assoc.t: Mary Jane, slang for marijuana
Mary Jane Watson, Spider-Man's love interest
Mary Janes, strapped flat shoes for girls
Mary Jane, peanut butter and molasses taffy candy

e.note: Mary Jane is widely known slang for marijuana.

e.etymology: A pet form of Dorothy, by way of Dot. Dorothy is the English form of Greek Dorothea, from doron, gift, and theos, God. Dottie is sometimes given as a full name.
namesakes: Dottie West (country singer)
Dottie Hinson (Geena Davis's catcher in A League of Their Own)
e.note: The spelling dotty is old British slang for eccentric or slightly mad.

e.etymology: The Arabic word for angel, from a Semitic root for a messenger that also gives Hebrew mal'akh. It is used for girls and, less often, boys; the Turkish form is Melek.
An Arabic name linked to hafs, a lion cub. It is best known from Hafsa bint Umar, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad and daughter of the caliph Umar, and is popular among Sunni Muslims.
The Spanish, Portuguese and Scandinavian form of Nathanael, from Hebrew Netan'el, God has given. In the Gospel of John, Nathanael is one of the first disciples.
namesakes: Natanael Cano (Mexican singer who popularized corridos tumbados)

e.etymology: A Scottish surname from places named with Gaelic ros, a promontory, or a related British word for a moor. It has been used as a first name since the early 19th century.
namesakes: Ross Geller (David Schwimmer's character on Friends)
Ross Perot (billionaire and 1992 presidential candidate)

assoc.t: Ross Dress for Less, off-price clothing store chain
Ross Geller, Rachel's on-again love on the sitcom Friends

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Latin Octavius, a Roman family name from octavus, eighth. Octavius was the birth name of the emperor Augustus.
namesakes: Octavio Paz (Mexican poet and Nobel laureate)

e.etymology: The name of the Roman goddess of love, from the Latin noun venus, loveliness or charm. The planet was named for the goddess, and the given name follows the goddess too.
namesakes: Venus Williams (tennis champion)

assoc.t: Venus, the Roman goddess of love and beauty
Venus, the second planet from the sun
Gillette Venus razors for women
Venus Williams, tennis champion

e.etymology: The English word pepper, from Latin piper and ultimately Sanskrit pippali. It began as a nickname for a lively person and as an occupational surname for a seller of the spice.
namesakes: Pepper Potts (Tony Stark's partner in Marvel's Iron Man films)

assoc.t: pepper, the spice and the vegetable
Dr Pepper soft drink
Sgt. Pepper, the Beatles' 1967 album

e.etymology: An English surname meaning son of Ann, which was a medieval short form of Agnes. It has been a first name since the 19th century and is also a favorite English name in Hong Kong.
namesakes: Anson Mount (actor in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds)
Anson Williams (Potsie on Happy Days)

e.etymology: A recent American spelling of Avianna, a name built in the 2000s on Ava with the -anna ending. It has no older meaning of its own.
A modern American name, a blend of Jasmine with the -lyn ending. It is also heard as a variant of Jazlyn or Jocelyn.
A phonetic respelling of Malachi, the Hebrew prophet's name meaning my messenger. The spelling also brings Malik and Kai to mind.
